title: doubt is my companion monster
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

I've had a very long, tumultuous relationship with self-doubt -- as my number one enemy, a villianous monster, a generous teacher, a loyal friend, and a companion for the twisty, dark paths of the creative life.

today, I'll share my own relationship with doubt, and offer a reframe for what doubt is -- not as contamination, or poison, not as something to fight or run away from, but as a essential friction for your life. I'll suggest a 3 part practice to work with doubt -- by creating spaciousness and containers to hold it, and to keep moving forwards, even (or especially) with doubt by your side.

doubt as the anti-hero

in the last episode, we explored clarity as not perfect opacity and good weather conditions, but as being in fluid moving conversation with your truth. today, I want to explore the anti-hero of this story that is self-doubt. and how when we do hard things, doubt is a force that can make us panic and feel paralyzed, push us into a corner to ask all the anxiety inducing questions of, am I on the right path? should I change course? am I doing something wrong?

the core question I want to explore today is, how do we move forwards when we feel doubt? and what is the deeper purpose and uses of doubt? can we reframe doubt as something that is generative instead of paralyzing?

when I was thinking about podcast episode topics and landed on the idea of doubt, it felt like coming full circle because when I was a high school senior, I wrote a commencement speech for my graduation about how doubt is the most generous of teachers. and now I'm not talking about school, I'm talking about the pathless, wild, creative path. but the relationship is the same.

doubt isn't the enemy, it's not poison that will contaminate everything. it's not a sign that you should stop and quit. it's not a villain monster that you need to run away from or destroy, destroy or be destroyed. the concept I'd like to share with you today is to think about doubt as a monster companion which will walk beside you and force you to choose, do I do this? do I try and maybe fail? or do I not walk forwards at all? do I go back? do I do something else?

I think the subject of doubt is so important. it's something we don't often speak about, but it is inevitable on any path, in any relationship, in any journey that you take. and instead of trying to control it, vanquish it, run from it, deny it, oppress it, what if we made space for it? what if we embraced it as a teacher, as a companion, as a guide?

what we think doubt is

so let's start by diving into what we commonly conceive of doubt as. I think that when I feel internal doubt, the first reaction is a sign, like maybe I'm doing something wrong and I should stop. maybe this doubt is like the first sign of getting a cold, like I should take lots of vitamin C, I should stop what I'm doing. and when I encounter external doubt from people in my world or my parents, the reaction that I feel is to feel shame and embarrassment and humiliation and rejection, or variations of that, or I'll feel very angry and how dare you doubt me.

a personal story, in 2018, I left my last job that I've ever had and started working for myself full-time as a creative person, hustling creative services to survive. and I grew up in an Asian immigrant family who invested money in my Ivy League diploma. my parents were materially supportive in that they gave me a financial safety net. at the same time, they doubted everything that I did and expressed their doubts.

my father might ask me to make a point and if his response was, quote, "I doubt it," it was probably one of the most triggering things I could ever hear in my life. and it would swing me into this extreme of defending my position with adamant warrior-like ferocity even if I myself would feel those doubts. or when my mother would say, "you're on the wrong path. you took the wrong turn and you should stop now," it would feel like I was at the beginning of a very long, difficult trek or marathon and I was tripping on my shoelaces before I've even taken a couple of steps.

so in responding to this external doubt, I felt like I had to act like I had zero doubt. I created these layers of defense mechanisms in which I would respond to doubt with such allergic reaction when in fact, of course I doubted everything that I did. of course, it was hard to keep going. even when my parents' voices weren't audible to me, they kept playing in my own internal radio system voices of not enough-ness, voices of stop now.

and when I tried to force my way through, when I tried to power through, sometimes even a dose, even a drop of doubt would feel crippling. as a result, I had to desensitize my capacity to feel. it was like I had to dull my senses because even feeling a little bit of doubt felt so dangerous to my nervous system. I had to become absolutist of right or wrong. and my reactions were very much knee-jerk reactions of either fight, like combat the doubt, or flight, run away from the doubt.

looking back, I think it is this relationship to doubt in the very early years of my creative journey that really depleted me and made the process of inhabiting myself feel so much harder than it could have been. and yet I don't regret any of it because I think I needed to know what that felt like before I could say with certainty that what I'm doing now, creating spaciousness for all the feelings and to keep going, is so much more nourishing and so much more sustainable to my system.

doubt as a part of the landscape

and so to reimagine or to recommit to a different relationship to doubt is to think of it as part of the landscape. when you're not climbing a ladder that someone else put in front of you, like a job or school or some kind of a system that is externally imposed, you will experience doubt. it is not a sign that you're in the wrong place. it's like the rocks or the hills or the shadows and the trees. it's useful friction. it forces you to walk through it, even when you're scared.

and so it's not about making doubt go away. it's not about being at war with doubt. it's about approaching it with curiosity and spaciousness and the capacity to hold it. it's inviting it to be a companion on your journey and asking, what can I learn from you? where do I feel resistance? where do I feel fear? how can I use you as a lens to look at what is actually true to me, what I truly value, what matters?

and then I think equally important is knowing that the feeling of doubt is not a constant state. if you are in the flow of movement long enough, your doubt will eventually resolve itself.

how I broke all the rules

as an example of how I experienced this, in the years I described to you, I, for a couple of years at the very beginning, I used to follow all the rules of how to be an artist on the internet, how to have a business. and then after I burnt out and felt very depleted and tired, I kind of just decided to ghost all the rules. I broke all of them because I had no energy to do them.

breaking the rules for me was in what I didn't do. no niche-ifying myself for digestibility, no social media for visibility, no emailing my network for work opportunities, no relationship marketing for expanding my reach, no platforms for discoverability, no lead magnets for conversion, no brochure-like website for sales, no consistency or very little consistency in my newsletters and no launch strategy for my offerings. and when I say strategy, what I mostly mean is I didn't sit down to plan what would be the most optimal, or maybe I did and then I never followed it anyway.

my quote-unquote strategy was built on doing only what nourishes my energy and nothing else. and I think as a side note, as a projector, I think part of the work is saying no to more things, even when there is so much doubt in my mind. questions, asking myself, am I being too hermity? am I crazy? am I going to fail? when my approach to sharing my work and having a business is so minimalist, literally just creating, sharing on my website and podcast, sending a newsletter and making offerings as if they're creative practices.

and yes, I might be missing out on building my audience, growing my business by not being on substack or not having a lead magnet, but the work is holding my own self-doubt, holding the doubt of others while doing my own thing and just committing to it because sustainability and being fully present in what I do is more important than any external strategy.

literally, I lived with doubt as to whether what I do would actually work for many, many years. every week, if not every day, sometimes it was very loud, very paralyzing, and sometimes where I would panic and wonder where the money would come from. but then I just kept moving forwards and clients would come from unexpected directions and I was able to focus on my creative work.

eventually, doubt became a part of the background noise. it was no longer a monster at full blast nuclear level amplitude. it was not something hiding in the shadows that could ambush me and attack me and undermine my every step. it became a companion. it was like taming this wild, chaotic, scary creature that could possibly kill me on the path. and allowing it to walk next to me as we took one step forwards at a time.

the practice

so what is the practice of making doubt your companion? how do you move forwards?

I think crucial to this process is not only to see it as friction for any creative landscape, but to trust that doubt happens in cycles. sometimes it will appear and feel very menacing. and then it will dissolve and then it will integrate into the atmosphere. you'll feel clarity, you'll feel the birds and then maybe they'll come back and you'll go through the same process. whether this applies to your creative work, your business, your life, your relationships, to everything, doubt has its own timeline.

the process of working with doubt, I see it as three parts: to normalize and acknowledge, to contain, and to move through it.

normalizing doubt

so normalizing doubt is to say, hello, you are here. it's acknowledging what can feel like a monster and acknowledging what relationship you have to the monster. when I started my podcast, probably every episode, there was a voice in me that was like, are they gonna understand what I'm talking about? do I make any sense? am I sure this is going to work? and the answer is, of course not. of course, I think maybe I make no sense, but somehow making space for doubt to exist makes it feel less oppressive.

so another example, maybe your doubt is, I'm sharing my work on my website, but I'm getting crickets and I'm wondering if I should go back to social media because it's not working or I don't feel like it's working. the first step is to acknowledge that that doubt, that questioning is so normal and you don't have to do anything urgent right at this moment, even if you feel this doubt.

containing doubt

then I would suggest containing it, creating a safe space to look at your doubt, to hold it, to make the monster feel a little more cozy without it destroying your life. you can feel doubt, you can hold your doubt and you can keep moving.

so what does holding it look like? it's acknowledging your feelings and examining your beliefs. maybe you feel lonely or FOMO or anxiety or scarcity when you're just on your website speaking to the void. maybe the underlying belief is, I won't connect to the people I want to connect to and therefore I will feel insignificant, therefore I won't be able to support myself.

and then after you hold the weight of all of those feelings and all the underlying beliefs, then you can start to ask gentle questions to explore what would be the worst thing that could happen? what does it mean for a practice to not work? what does working mean? and what does your system really need right now that you can get or not get from different platforms or spaces?

and then after you explore to remember to regulate your nervous system, ask yourself, how can I feel safe and supported as I'm walking this path, as I'm in the figuring out process?

moving with doubt

after you've acknowledged doubt, work to hold and contain the doubt, then it's like the monster can walk beside you. you can design experiments, containers, you can ask it questions. you can say, okay, I'm feeling doubtful about sharing on my website to the void, but I feel like I want to do it. so I'm gonna try it for 30 days every day, keep a log and see how I feel. and I know that I need connection in other ways. so let me experiment with creating a newsletter or asking some friends to form a community.

I think there's a simultaneous approach of being able to hold the complexity of the issue, all the doubt, all the fear, all the second guessing, all the what ifs, at the same time, to make the movement forward a binary equation, one step forwards, zero or one, either you go forwards or you stay where you are. and when I say binary equation, I mean, you can decide, you can commit to taking the next step without committing to one path the entire way. I decide to do something until I don't feel like committing to it anymore, but the commitment is 100% presence. measured one step one day at a time.

it's holding the paradox of being able to have all of these doubts and being able to move forwards. and the reason for this is because when you move forwards, whatever you discover, whatever you learn, you'll integrate that, you'll use that to inform your next step.

befriending the monster

if you practice walking forwards with doubt as your companion monster, over time, you will notice how it will shape shift and lead you down a different path.

working with doubt is about befriending it. it's about saying, yes, this is hard. you will make the road much more challenging and interesting for me. I will experience friction. I will experience pain. part of the work is that monsters are scary. monsters trigger, are triggering all of our childhood fears, but the goal isn't to slay you or to run away from you. it's not to be doubt free. it's to let it walk beside you, to hold it close to your heart as a part of your landscape and to say, yes, you are here. I'm not afraid of you. you will help me walk this path and you'll keep me company, even or especially on the darkest of nights.
